title: The ULTIMATE Shoulder Exercises Tier-List (Boulder-tier to Pebble-tier)
summary: He ranks 65 shoulder exercises from Boulder tier (S) to Pebble tier (D), weighing hypertrophy alongside shoulder health and stimulus-to-fatigue. Strict barbell OHP, cable lateral raises, handstand push-ups, machine shoulder press, trap bar OHP, close-grip incline press, dips, decline ring push-ups and the power raise are top picks; momentum lifts and gimmicks sit at the bottom.
claims: Tiers: Boulder (S), excellent (A), decent (B), mediocre (C), Pebble (D); ranking considers hypertrophy, shoulder health, mobility and stimulus-to-fatigue, comparing lifts within the same family
Strict barbell overhead press done from a rack is Boulder tier; cleaning it from the floor wastes energy and stability
Seated or standing makes no difference for shoulder pressing as long as legs are not involved; choose by lower-back comfort (seated bothers his back)
The Z press is mediocre: being less stable and lifting less weight does not recruit the shoulders more
Do raises slow and controlled; lateral raises are not dangerous done properly, but treating them as a compound with swinging can wreck the rotator cuff
Lean-away (Egyptian) unilateral lateral raises are excellent: leaning prevents shrugging and keeps tension through the useful range
Cable lateral raises are the best lateral raise (S tier) due to constant tension; do them however you best feel the delt
Lu raises are only A tier: overhyped, limit load and wrist/grip comfort, though great for mobility and small rear shoulder muscles
Push-ups rank higher for shoulders the more the torso is vertical and the range is increased: pike C, deficit B, decline A, handstand push-up S
The bottom of the overhead press is where shoulder recruitment peaks; pin presses skip it, so the higher the pin the worse
Push press is mediocre: legs move the supramaximal load and you skip the negative
Shoulders need a middle ground: implements that fix the path too much or allow too much 3D freedom (like the landmine press) can cause tendinitis
Trap bar overhead press is S tier for those who dislike straight-bar pressing: neutral grip and more range; grip the frame, not the handles
Reverse flies (seated or on an incline bench) are A tier: they counter internal rotation, hit mid and lower traps and help press stability; use much less weight than laterals
Front raises are not useless since every delt head works in any raise, but they are redundant with presses; prioritize lateral raises to avoid reinforcing an already strong front delt
Behind-the-neck press is A tier if controlled: he stopped at the bump behind his head and never had shoulder issues; use a Smith machine if worried
Combination lifts like the Cuban press fail because each shoulder function needs a different load
A plain machine shoulder press is S tier and could be your only press; whatever puts the muscle under tension is good
Rows can train the rear delt, but do both rows and raises; rear delt rows are only B tier because traps and upper back take work
A weak rear delt makes the shoulder look worse because it gives the shoulder its pop
There is no single correct face pull form; do them however feels good and hits the rear delt
Ring face pulls beat cable face pulls (S tier) because bodyweight keeps loading the eccentric while a cable stack unloads
Shadow boxing with heavy dumbbells is dangerous: at full extension the rotator cuff alone handles the load
Dumbbell external rotations are useless because tension vanishes at the top; use cables or face pulls
Every shoulder injury comes from misunderstanding its structure and how it responds to loads
Upright rows are safe and A tier if done for 10-15 reps with a manageable weight
Reverse pec deck is S tier for rear delts; put the hand behind the handle and push with the wrist rather than gripping to avoid biceps tendon stress
If you want bigger shoulders you must do vertical presses
In raises, the more the torso is bent the more rear delt and back; in presses, the more inclined the body the more chest
A burn (battle ropes, washing hair) means fast fiber activation, not a good hypertrophy stimulus
Swimming builds big shoulders but takes 5-10 times the time to match an overhead press stimulus and makes the physique disproportionate
Bench press trains the shoulders but delt activation competes with pecs, so B tier
Incline presses beyond a slight incline are more shoulder than chest (A tier); close-grip incline press is S tier for deeper shoulder flexion but riskier, so build up gradually
Most people stop the overhead press too high; going deeper into shoulder flexion is where most gains are
Shrugs are a trap exercise, not shoulders, and do not belong on a shoulder list
Strongman shoulder development comes from pressing and from heavy pulls/carries that stretch delts and traps
Dips are S tier and could build massive chest and shoulders alone, but are riskier than presses because there is no safety net at the bottom
Decline ring push-ups with a vertical torso are S tier: safe on wrists and elbows with a perfect stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
Gada swings are B tier: not for hypertrophy but good for shoulder mobility and health
Rear delt swings (heavy dumbbells, chest supported, small motions) are A tier for advanced rear delt work, learned from John Meadows; straps may be needed
The key to big shoulders is finding 5-10 lifts you can progressively overload for 10 years and stay excited about, not doing them all
The forearm tier list is next and forearms have become his favourite muscle to train
